common_name: L'Avvenire Camellia (Antique French Pink Formal Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to establish before the mid-to-late season flush.

directions: L'Avvenire ('The Future') is an antique Camellia japonica raised by the Guichard Soeurs nursery of Nantes, France and catalogued in the 1890s, bearing solid pink, formal double flowers on a slow-growing, compact shrub. It survives in cultivation mainly as the un-variegated parent of the stable marbled sport long sold as 'Lallarook' (or 'Lalla Rookh'), which carries the same flower form streaked in white. Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and prune only lightly right after flowering, since camellias set next year's buds on the current season's growth.

common_name: Gubijin Japanese Iris (Classic Heirloom Reddish-Purple Iris ensata)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, organic, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun.

directions: Gubijin ('beautiful lady', a name referencing the legendary Consort Yu) is a traditional Japanese iris long grown in Japan's Higo and Edo ensata lines, bearing large, flat-faced, reddish-purple flowers with a paler central ray on broad, overlapping falls. It survives today partly as a parent in modern pseudata breeding, appearing in hybridizer Jill Copeland's seedling GXS-2 (crossed with the cultivar 'Sushi'), one parent behind her American Dykes Medal-winning 'Alabama Blue Fin'. Like other Japanese iris it wants full sun and constantly moist to wet, acidic soil through the growing season, and resents the dry, alkaline conditions that bearded iris tolerate easily. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring or right after bloom to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Sushi Japanese Iris (Parent of Alabama Blue Fin)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, organic, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun.

directions: Sushi is a modern Iris ensata cultivar used by hybridizer Jill Copeland as a parent, crossed with the classic cultivar 'Gubijin', to produce seedling GXS-2, one parent behind her American Dykes Medal-winning pseudata introduction 'Alabama Blue Fin'. Like other Japanese iris it wants full sun and constantly moist, slightly acidic soil through spring and summer, and resists the alkaline, fast-draining conditions that suit bearded iris. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring, keeping the planting site reliably damp through the growing season.

common_name: Christina's Sister Pseudata Iris (Parent of Alabama Blue Fin)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, organic soil kept consistently moist to wet.

directions: Christina's Sister is a pseudata iris, part of the hybrid group descended from crosses between Iris ensata and the wetland species Iris pseudacorus, grown today chiefly for its role as a parent crossed with seedling GXS-2 to produce hybridizer Jill Copeland's 'Alabama Blue Fin', the 2026 American Dykes Medal winner. Like other pseudata iris it wants rich, organic soil kept consistently moist to wet through the growing season, tolerating standing water better than bearded iris while still appreciating good drainage in winter. Plant divisions in spring and keep the planting site reliably damp, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years.

common_name: Poet's Dream Bearded Iris (Historic Parent of Winter Olympics)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Poet's Dream is a mid-20th-century Tall Bearded iris, grown today mainly for its place in iris pedigree as a parent, crossed with 'Eleanor's Pride', of Opal Brown's 'Winter Olympics', registered in 1961 and later honored with the American Dykes Medal. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rot far more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting the healthiest outer rhizomes.

common_name: Fairy Ring Bearded Iris (Parent of Rimaround)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil.

directions: Fairy Ring is a Tall Bearded iris grown today mainly for its role in iris pedigree as a parent, crossed with 'Art Deco', of J. Terry Aitken's 2007 introduction 'Rimaround', winner of the American Iris Society's Hans and Jacob Sass Medal in 2013. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting the healthiest outer rhizomes.

common_name: Sarah Tiffney Siberian Iris (Parent of Here Be Dragons)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Sarah Tiffney is a Siberian iris bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks of Joe Pye Weed's Garden in Carlisle, Massachusetts, grown today chiefly for its breeding legacy as the seed parent crossed with 'Tom Schaefer' to produce the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal-winning 'Here Be Dragons' in 2010. Like other Siberian iris it tolerates consistently moist to wet soil far better than bearded types and rarely suffers from rot or iris borer. Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade, and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since flowering improves as they mature.

common_name: Tom Schaefer Siberian Iris (Parent of Here Be Dragons)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Tom Schaefer is a Siberian iris bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks of Joe Pye Weed's Garden, used as the pollen parent crossed with 'Sarah Tiffney' to produce the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal-winning 'Here Be Dragons' in 2010. Grown on its own, it offers the same easy, trouble-free character typical of Siberian iris, with narrow, grassy foliage that stays tidy through the growing season after bloom. Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade, and divide congested clumps only once flowering begins to decline in an overcrowded center.

common_name: Doblefina Blood Orange (Historic Spanish Blood Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, protecting young trees from hard freezes.

directions: Doblefina is an early 20th-century Spanish blood orange grown around Valencia, valued for moderately pigmented red-streaked flesh and juice, firm texture, and a sweet-tart flavor milder than deeply colored blood oranges like Moro. It survives today chiefly as the parent of the seedless bud mutation 'Sanguinelli', which arose from it in the late 1920s and has since become the more widely planted selection. Grow it like other sweet oranges, in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil, feeding with a citrus fertilizer program through the growing season. Fruit colors and sweetens through winter and holds well on the tree, so harvest as needed rather than all at once.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Siamese Pink Pummelo (Historic Parent of Chandler Pummelo)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, protecting young trees from frost.

directions: Siamese Pink is a Southeast Asian heirloom pummelo used by University of California Riverside breeders Cameron and Soost as one of the two parents, crossed with 'Siamese Sweet', in the 1961 release of 'Chandler' pummelo. Like other pummelos it grows into a large, vigorous citrus tree bearing oversized, thick-rinded fruit that needs a long, warm season to mature fully. Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and protect young trees from frost, since pummelos are among the least cold-hardy citrus types. Established trees benefit from fruit thinning in heavy years to maintain size.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Siamese Sweet Pummelo (Historic Parent of Chandler Pummelo)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, protecting young trees from frost.

directions: Siamese Sweet is a Southeast Asian heirloom pummelo used by University of California Riverside breeders Cameron and Soost as one of the two parents, crossed with 'Siamese Pink', in the 1961 release of 'Chandler' pummelo. As its name suggests it was valued chiefly for notably low acidity and a sweet flavor compared with the sharper, more acidic pummelo types common at the time. Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and protect young trees from hard freezes, since pummelos tolerate less cold than mandarins or sweet oranges. Established trees need little care beyond routine citrus fertilizing and occasional thinning of the oversized fruit.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
